eaOps

v26.9.2
Multi-Cloud|AI-native enterprise architecture operations (eaOps) — for both product delivery and service engagements.

eaOps (Multi-Cloud|AI-native Enterprise Architecture Operations) is a reference checklist for the capabilities an enterprise architect needs to plan for, grounded throughout in a single hypothetical use case — Customer, Products & Orders (CPO) — so every item has a concrete example behind it rather than staying abstract.

The document's own structure is 10 Ops, each broken into Functions, each broken into Parameters — every Parameter carrying four parallel descriptions (Azure, GCP, AWS, open-source) so the same capability is never tied to one vendor.

Block Diagram Of eaOps

Top 10 eaOps

1Business

Op 1 covers the business case for CPO before any architecture gets built. 1.1 Business Architecture is the financial and contractual foundation — ROI/TCO modeling, build-vs-buy analysis, pricing and SLA definitions, error budgets, and the outsourced-engagement artifacts (SOW, Engagement Billing Model) that apply when the work is contracted out. 1.2 FinOps & Cost Optimization is the ongoing cost discipline once it's built — cloud cost dashboards, IaC cost estimation, reserved capacity, AI token spend tracking, and the FinOps practice that ties it together.

1.1.11Statement of Work (SOW)
1.1.11.azureApplies to outsourced/vendor-built engagements only — formal scope, deliverables, milestones, and acceptance criteria for a third-party delivery contract. In-house builds use Build vs. Buy Analysis, Sprint/Backlog, ADRs and ARB instead — no SOW needed.
1.1.11.gcpApplies to outsourced/vendor-built engagements only — formal scope, deliverables, milestones, and acceptance criteria for a third-party delivery contract. In-house builds use Build vs. Buy Analysis, Sprint/Backlog, ADRs and ARB instead — no SOW needed.
1.1.11.awsApplies to outsourced/vendor-built engagements only — formal scope, deliverables, milestones, and acceptance criteria for a third-party delivery contract. In-house builds use Build vs. Buy Analysis, Sprint/Backlog, ADRs and ARB instead — no SOW needed.
1.1.11.open-sourceApplies to outsourced/vendor-built engagements only — formal scope, deliverables, milestones, and acceptance criteria for a third-party delivery contract. In-house builds use Build vs. Buy Analysis, Sprint/Backlog, ADRs and ARB instead — no SOW needed.
1.1.12Engagement Billing Model
1.1.12.azureApplies to outsourced/vendor engagements only (CPO paying a vendor to build, or CPO billing its own clients for delivered services) — Time & Materials vs Fixed-Price vs Retainer billing structure. In-house work has no external bill — cost is tracked internally via Chargeback Model instead.
1.1.12.gcpApplies to outsourced/vendor engagements only (CPO paying a vendor to build, or CPO billing its own clients for delivered services) — Time & Materials vs Fixed-Price vs Retainer billing structure. In-house work has no external bill — cost is tracked internally via Chargeback Model instead.
1.1.12.awsApplies to outsourced/vendor engagements only (CPO paying a vendor to build, or CPO billing its own clients for delivered services) — Time & Materials vs Fixed-Price vs Retainer billing structure. In-house work has no external bill — cost is tracked internally via Chargeback Model instead.

2Stake Holders

Op 2 covers everyone outside core engineering with a stake in CPO. 2.1 Customer Success is the external-facing side — status pages, support ticketing, onboarding/UAT flows, sandbox environments, white-labelling, and the client engagement portal for service-delivery clients. 2.2 Executive & Cross-Department Visibility is the internal reporting side — executive KPI dashboards, weekly digests, a data catalog, and self-service analytics/experimentation for other teams. 2.3 Skill & Resource Management is the staffing side — a skills matrix, hiring-gap analysis, and training budget, following the same build-vs-buy fork applied to people instead of software.

3.1.6Self-Hosted GPU Infrastructure
3.1.6.azureOwn GPU compute (AKS GPU node pools) for open-weight/SLM models — only if self-hosting replaces Azure OpenAI, monitored via Tech Radar — itself a Build vs. Buy Analysis decision applied to infrastructure (own hardware vs. managed AI API). Exception to this document's serverless-first stance: GPU workloads need node-level hardware access; serverless GPU support (Cloud Run, Container Apps) is still limited/immature as of this writing.
3.1.6.gcpOwn GPU compute (GKE GPU node pools) for open-weight/SLM models — only if self-hosting replaces Vertex AI, monitored via Tech Radar — itself a Build vs. Buy Analysis decision applied to infrastructure (own hardware vs. managed AI API). Exception to this document's serverless-first stance: GPU workloads need node-level hardware access; serverless GPU support (Cloud Run, Container Apps) is still limited/immature as of this writing.
3.1.6.awsOwn GPU compute (EKS GPU node pools) for open-weight/SLM models — only if self-hosting replaces Amazon Bedrock, monitored via Tech Radar — itself a Build vs. Buy Analysis decision applied to infrastructure (own hardware vs. managed AI API). Exception to this document's serverless-first stance: GPU workloads need node-level hardware access; serverless GPU support (Cloud Run, Container Apps) is still limited/immature as of this writing.
3.1.6.open-sourceOwn GPU compute (Kubernetes GPU node pools, on-prem or bare-metal) for open-weight/SLM models — only if self-hosting replaces managed AI APIs, monitored via Tech Radar — itself a Build vs. Buy Analysis decision applied to infrastructure (own hardware vs. managed AI API). Exception to this document's serverless-first stance: GPU workloads need node-level hardware access; serverless GPU support (Cloud Run, Container Apps) is still limited/immature as of this writing.

4Operations & Governance

Op 4 is how CPO stays reliable and disciplined once it's running. 4.1 SRE & Operations is the reliability operating model — SLOs/error budgets, incident response, on-call, postmortems, DR testing, and capacity planning, plus the runbook for executing outsourced/client engagements themselves. 4.2 Architecture Governance is the decision-making discipline — C4 diagrams, ADRs, coding/design standards, API and UI/DB design guidelines, and the Architecture Review Board gate that also covers vendor-proposed technology in outsourced work. 4.3 Change & Release Management is how changes actually ship — release calendars, canary/blue-green rollout, the Change Advisory Board, and Definition of Done/Ready. 4.4 Migration & Upgrade Management is planned technical change — schema migrations, framework upgrades, API deprecation, and cloud migration strategy (the 7 Rs).

4.2.7.gcpREST conventions, versioning, error formats — .NET APIs: ASP.NET Core Middleware pipeline (cross-cutting concerns), Unit of Work pattern (EF Core DbContext), Repository pattern (Repository<T> over DbSet<T>); Data Annotations/FluentValidation for validation, built-in ProblemDetails for RFC7807 error responses
4.2.7.awsREST conventions, versioning, error formats — .NET APIs: ASP.NET Core Middleware pipeline (cross-cutting concerns), Unit of Work pattern (EF Core DbContext), Repository pattern (Repository<T> over DbSet<T>); Data Annotations/FluentValidation for validation, built-in ProblemDetails for RFC7807 error responses
4.2.7.open-sourceREST conventions, versioning, error formats — Python: FastAPI/Django middleware, SQLAlchemy Unit of Work + Repository pattern; Pydantic validation + RFC7807 error responses via FastAPI. Java: Spring Boot interceptors/filters, JPA EntityManager as Unit of Work, Spring Data Repository; Bean Validation + @ControllerAdvice/ProblemDetail for RFC7807 errors. Node.js: Express/Koa middleware, Prisma/TypeORM Unit of Work + Repository pattern; Zod/Joi validation + error-handling middleware

5Security & Compliance

Op 5 covers security end to end. 5.1 Identity & Governance is who can access what — IdP, RBAC/workload identity, secrets management, privileged identity, and conditional access. 5.2 DevSecOps is security built into the pipeline — SAST, SCA, container scanning, and DevOps security posture management. 5.3 Security Operations (SecOps) is live threat monitoring — SIEM, CSPM, XDR, and on-call alerting integration. 5.4 Penetration Testing & Ethical Hacking is adversarial validation — OWASP ZAP, manual and third-party pen testing, vulnerability disclosure, bug bounty, and red team/blue team exercises. 5.5 License Compliance is open-source license risk — scanning, policy, and a combined vulnerability/license gate. 5.6 EOL & Package Management is dependency lifecycle — EOL tracking, automated updates, and vulnerability policy.

6Non-AI Engineering

Op 6 is the full engineering stack, entity by entity and layer by layer — serverless-primary throughout, with Kubernetes/VMs only as an explicit secondary path. 6.1 Traffic & Networking — CDN, DDoS protection, load balancing, rate limiting. 6.2 Frontend — the client stack across web/desktop/mobile/wearable/TV. 6.3 Gateway & API Management — API gateway, versioning, feature flags, developer portal, GraphQL. 6.4 Backend Services — the Customer/Product/Order/Audit/Identity APIs plus multi-tenancy, sagas, and dead-letter handling. 6.5 Data & Messaging — database choice, caching, the event bus, and BI. 6.6 Resilience & Reliability — retry/circuit-breaker, health checks, autoscaling, multi-AZ HA, chaos engineering. 6.7 Observability — tracing, monitoring, OpenTelemetry, log aggregation. 6.8 Testing & Quality — unit through E2E and performance testing. 6.9 Localization & Accessibility — i18n/l10n, RTL, timezones. 6.10 Infrastructure & Cost — container registry/runtime, CI/CD, IaC, cost optimization. 6.11 Developer Experience — local dev setup and AI coding assistants. 6.12 Cross-Cell/Service Integration ties it together — the cell-based architecture pattern and the full Customer/Product/Order CRUD event set that powers 8.7's multi-agent workflow.

7AI Integration & Migration

Op 7 splits it into three paths: 7.1 AI-Legacy Integration bolts AI onto the legacy system from outside — a sidecar/facade wraps it (7.1.1), a CDC pipeline feeds its quality-checked, PII-redacted data into a vector store for RAG (7.1.2, 7.1.4), and API-fication exposes it via REST/MCP so AI agents can call it as a tool (7.1.3) — none of this touches the legacy code itself. 7.2 AI-Native Migration is the actual upgrade: the Strangler Fig pattern incrementally swaps out legacy rule-based logic for an ML/LLM reasoning module one piece at a time, guarded by parallel-run validation, a fallback circuit breaker, human-in-the-loop escalation for low-confidence calls, and post-cutover drift monitoring (7.2.2–7.2.5) before the legacy logic is fully replaced. 7.3 AI-Assisted Code Migration is a different axis — using AI coding assistants to accelerate the migration work itself (translating legacy code, generating a golden regression suite, recovering lost documentation), independent of whether the target system ends up AI-native.

7.1AI-Legacy Integration
7.1.1AI Sidecar / Facade Pattern
7.1.1.azureWrap a legacy app with an AI layer (Azure API Management facade + Azure AI Service alongside it) without touching legacy internals
7.1.1.gcpWrap a legacy app with an AI layer (Apigee facade + Vertex AI service alongside it) without touching legacy internals
7.1.1.awsWrap a legacy app with an AI layer (Amazon API Gateway facade + Amazon Bedrock service alongside it) without touching legacy internals
7.1.1.open-sourceWrap a legacy app with an AI layer (FastAPI facade + LangChain service alongside it) without touching legacy internals
7.1.2Legacy Data Pipeline for RAG
7.1.2.azureAzure Data Factory + CDC — extract from legacy databases (mainframe, on-prem SQL Server, COBOL systems) into Azure AI Search vector store for RAG
7.1.2.gcpCloud Datastream (CDC) + Dataflow — extract from legacy databases (mainframe, on-prem SQL Server, COBOL systems) into Vertex AI Search vector store for RAG
7.1.2.awsAWS Database Migration Service (DMS CDC) + Glue — extract from legacy databases (mainframe, on-prem SQL Server, COBOL systems) into Amazon OpenSearch Service (vector engine) for RAG
7.1.2.open-sourceAirbyte / Debezium (open-source CDC) — extract from legacy databases into Weaviate/Qdrant vector store for RAG
7.1.3API-fication of Legacy Systems
7.1.3.azureAzure API Management + Logic Apps — expose legacy systems via modern REST/MCP so AI agents can call them as tools
7.1.3.gcpApigee + Cloud Workflows — expose legacy systems via modern REST/MCP so AI agents can call them as tools
7.1.3.awsAmazon API Gateway + Step Functions — expose legacy systems via modern REST/MCP so AI agents can call them as tools
7.1.3.open-sourceKong/Traefik + FastAPI wrapper — expose legacy systems via modern REST/MCP so AI agents can call them as tools
7.1.4Legacy Data Quality & PII Redaction for AI
7.1.4.azureData quality remediation (dedup, schema normalization) + Azure AI Language PII detection/redaction on legacy data before RAG ingestion or model training
7.1.4.gcpData quality remediation (dedup, schema normalization) + Cloud Data Loss Prevention (DLP) API PII detection/redaction on legacy data before RAG ingestion or model training
7.1.4.awsData quality remediation (dedup, schema normalization) + Amazon Comprehend PII detection/redaction on legacy data before RAG ingestion or model training
7.1.4.open-sourceData quality remediation (dedup, schema normalization) + Microsoft Presidio (open-source) PII detection/redaction on legacy data before RAG ingestion or model training
7.2AI-Native Migration (Strangler Fig)
7.2.1AI-Native Rewrite (Strangler Fig for AI)
7.2.1.azureIncrementally replace legacy rule-based/procedural logic with an ML model or LLM-based reasoning module — one legacy module at a time, shadow-mode validation before cutover, via Azure App Configuration feature flags
7.2.1.gcpIncrementally replace legacy rule-based/procedural logic with an ML model or LLM-based reasoning module — one legacy module at a time, shadow-mode validation before cutover, via Firebase Remote Config / Parameter Manager feature flags
7.2.1.awsIncrementally replace legacy rule-based/procedural logic with an ML model or LLM-based reasoning module — one legacy module at a time, shadow-mode validation before cutover, via AWS AppConfig feature flags
7.2.1.open-sourceIncrementally replace legacy rule-based/procedural logic with an ML model or LLM-based reasoning module — one legacy module at a time, shadow-mode validation before cutover, via Unleash/Flagsmith feature flags
7.2.2Parallel-Run / Shadow Validation
7.2.2.azureDual-invoke legacy and AI logic on live traffic, logging both outputs to Application Insights for offline comparison without acting on the AI result — validates accuracy before cutover
7.2.2.gcpDual-invoke legacy and AI logic on live traffic, logging both outputs to Cloud Monitoring for offline comparison without acting on the AI result — validates accuracy before cutover
7.2.2.awsDual-invoke legacy and AI logic on live traffic, logging both outputs to Amazon CloudWatch for offline comparison without acting on the AI result — validates accuracy before cutover
7.2.2.open-sourceDual-invoke legacy and AI logic on live traffic, logging both outputs to Prometheus + Grafana (open-source) for offline comparison without acting on the AI result — validates accuracy before cutover
7.2.3Fallback / Circuit Breaker to Legacy Logic
7.2.3.azurePolly circuit breaker routes back to the original rule-based logic when the AI service is unavailable, times out, or returns below-threshold confidence

8AI-Native Engineering

Where Op 7 is about touching AI onto legacy systems, Op 8 is the AI stack itself. 8.1 AI Services is the app-facing layer — the SDK/agent code calls (8.1.1–8.1.6, single- and multi-agent) plus the safety and quality gates around them (AI Guardrails, AI Red Teaming, Prompt Versioning, AI Evals, Prompt Sanitization — 8.1.7–8.1.11). 8.2 AI Platform is what backs those calls — the model, search/RAG, storage, and OCR services. 8.3 AI Capacity & Governance is the operational layer on top — capacity reservations, quota/region planning, model lifecycle tracking, network isolation, data residency, and human-in-the-loop override controls. 8.4 Responsible AI is the ethics/fairness layer, distinct from 8.3's ops governance — bias testing, explainability documentation, user-facing transparency disclosure, and a review-board/impact-assessment gate for high-risk AI features before they ship. 8.5 AI DevOps & Delivery Pipeline is how AI changes actually ship — continuous security monitoring (AISecOps), a prompt/model-aware CI/CD pipeline, tracing/debugging, a dev sandbox, human QA review, and canary/shadow rollout with auto-rollback. 8.6 AI Deployment & Channels is where the shipped AI capability actually runs and how users reach it — inference pattern, multi-region deployment, and the delivery surfaces (in-app, chat platforms, voice/IVR, partner API). 8.7 CPO Multi-Agent Workflow puts it all together as a worked example, using the Agent → Skill → Tool pattern: a Customer, Product, and Order Agent (8.7.1–8.7.3), the Skills they share instead of reimplement (8.7.4), and two complementary coordination paths — async, driven by the 6.12 CRUD events (8.7.5), and sync, via a top-level orchestrator (8.7.6).

8.7.5Event-Driven Multi-Agent Workflow
8.7.5.azureThe CPO CRUD events (6.12.3–6.12.14) are the async coordination bus between agents, per 8.1.5 Agent Choreography — no direct agent-to-agent calls. Example: Order Agent's place_order tool publishes 6.12.11 OrderCreated; Customer Agent subscribes and reacts by re-evaluating loyalty tier within its Profile Management Skill, fully decoupled from the Order Agent's request/response cycle

8.7.6CPO Orchestrator Agent
8.7.6.azureThe top-level agent a channel (8.6) actually talks to; synchronously routes one user request across 8.7.1–8.7.3's domain agents and their Skills using 8.1.3 Multi-Agent Workflow (orchestrator-worker pattern) + 8.2.2 Model Router — complements 8.7.5's async event path rather than replacing it. Worked example: "where's my order, and can I get a discount on my next one?" routes to Order Agent (get_order_status), Product Agent (recommend_products), and Customer Agent (check loyalty tier) in parallel, then composes one reply

95 Year Vision

Op 9 is forward-looking, not built or committed — distinct from Op 3's watch-list of external technologies being tracked, this is the trajectory of CPO's own architecture over the next five years. 9.1 Platform Evolution is where the built system (Ops 1–6) is headed — multi-tenant SaaS, genuine active-active multi-cloud, CPO exposed as a developer platform, and periodic outsource-vs-insource rebalancing as it matures. 9.2 AI Maturity Roadmap is where the AI capability (Ops 7–8) is headed — completing the Strangler Fig legacy sunset, bounded autonomous agent operations, a self-optimizing eval/deployment loop, and the CPO Orchestrator Agent maturing into a full planner.

9.1.1Multi-Tenant SaaS Transition

10The Black Box

Op 10 is a forensic capability, not an operational one — modeled on an aircraft's flight recorder, built specifically to answer "what happened right before this crashed," not to monitor day-to-day health (that's 6.7 Observability) or log business changes (that's 6.4.6 Audit API). 10.1 System Flight Data Recorder is the technical half — continuous, tamper-evident state capture in storage isolated from the systems it records, so it survives the very incident it exists to explain. 10.2 AI Cockpit Voice Recorder is the AI-specific half — the complete reasoning trail behind every agent action (8.7), captured immutably so an agent's bad decision can be replayed and understood after the fact, not just monitored while it's happening.

10.1System Flight Data Recorder
10.1.1Immutable State Snapshot Capture
10.1.1.azureContinuous, fine-grained capture of request/system state (inputs, decision points, resource state) at every service boundary — independent of and outliving the normal observability stack (6.7 Observability), analogous to a flight data recorder's continuous technical telemetry
10.1.1.gcpContinuous, fine-grained capture of request/system state (inputs, decision points, resource state) at every service boundary — independent of and outliving the normal observability stack (6.7 Observability), analogous to a flight data recorder's continuous technical telemetry
10.1.1.awsContinuous, fine-grained capture of request/system state (inputs, decision points, resource state) at every service boundary — independent of and outliving the normal observability stack (6.7 Observability), analogous to a flight data recorder's continuous technical telemetry
10.1.1.open-sourceContinuous, fine-grained capture of request/system state (inputs, decision points, resource state) at every service boundary — independent of and outliving the normal observability stack (6.7 Observability), analogous to a flight data recorder's continuous technical telemetry
10.1.2Stall/Crash Recoverability
10.1.2.azureStall detection — early degradation signals (rising latency, circuit-breaker trips per 6.6.1 Resilience Library, dropping agent confidence) trigger an auto-recovery attempt before a full crash. If recovery fails, the Black Box's own storage (Azure Blob Storage with an immutability policy, WORM/legal hold) sits in an account isolated from the services it records, so it survives the crash itself — the way an aircraft's FDR is built to survive impact
10.1.2.gcpStall detection — early degradation signals (rising latency, circuit-breaker trips per 6.6.1 Resilience Library, dropping agent confidence) trigger an auto-recovery attempt before a full crash. If recovery fails, the Black Box's own storage (Google Cloud Storage with Bucket Lock, WORM) sits in a project isolated from the services it records, so it survives the crash itself — the way an aircraft's FDR is built to survive impact
10.1.2.awsStall detection — early degradation signals (rising latency, circuit-breaker trips per 6.6.1 Resilience Library, dropping agent confidence) trigger an auto-recovery attempt before a full crash. If recovery fails, the Black Box's own storage (Amazon S3 with Object Lock, WORM) sits in an account isolated from the services it records, so it survives the crash itself — the way an aircraft's FDR is built to survive impact
10.1.2.open-sourceStall detection — early degradation signals (rising latency, circuit-breaker trips per 6.6.1 Resilience Library, dropping agent confidence) trigger an auto-recovery attempt before a full crash. If recovery fails, the Black Box's own storage (MinIO with Object Lock, open-source S3-compatible WORM) sits isolated from the services it records, so it survives the crash itself — the way an aircraft's FDR is built to survive impact
10.1.3Time-Synchronized Timeline Reconstruction
10.1.3.azureCorrelates Black Box captures across every involved service and agent into a single chronological incident timeline — distinct from 6.7.4 Centralized Log Aggregation's live, searchable operational logs; assembled only during a formal investigation to answer what led up to the crash
10.1.3.gcpCorrelates Black Box captures across every involved service and agent into a single chronological incident timeline — distinct from 6.7.4 Centralized Log Aggregation's live, searchable operational logs; assembled only during a formal investigation to answer what led up to the crash
10.1.3.awsCorrelates Black Box captures across every involved service and agent into a single chronological incident timeline — distinct from 6.7.4 Centralized Log Aggregation's live, searchable operational logs; assembled only during a formal investigation to answer what led up to the crash
10.1.3.open-sourceCorrelates Black Box captures across every involved service and agent into a single chronological incident timeline — distinct from 6.7.4 Centralized Log Aggregation's live, searchable operational logs; assembled only during a formal investigation to answer what led up to the crash

10.1.4.awsTightly scoped, fully audited access to Black Box data — granted only during a formal incident investigation (feeds 4.1.3 Incident Response Playbook and 4.1.6 Postmortem Process), not available for routine debugging, mirroring the legally protected access model around aviation FDR/CVR data

10.2.4Black Box Immutability Guarantee
